app.name: Gmail
app.canDo: Read, sort and label email, write draft replies and send messages from the inboxes that users connect.

oauth.notes: You set up the app in Google Cloud. Other Google APIs use the same steps. But Google controls the Gmail permissions to read email more strictly than most.

verdict.summary: You can make the app in minutes. But Google calls access to read or change email 'restricted'. Google must verify your app. If your servers get that email, an approved assessor must audit you each year. This takes weeks.

whoYouNeed.role: A person who can change the DNS of your company domain
whoYouNeed.why: Google must see proof that you own the domain of your home page and privacy policy.

whoYouNeed.role: A person who can approve costs
whoYouNeed.why: A third-party assessor does the security assessment each year. Google does not publish the cost.

whoYouNeed.role: A person to record a demo video
whoYouNeed.why: Google wants a video of the sign-in steps. The video must also show how you use each restricted permission.

steps.title: Sign in to Google Cloud and create a project
steps.plain: Sign in to console.cloud.google.com with a company account. Create a project for your app.
steps.whyHuman: You must sign in yourself. You must also accept the Google Cloud terms yourself.

sources.title: Google: Create a Google Cloud project

steps.title: Turn on the Gmail API
steps.plain: In the project, open the API Library. Find the Gmail API and enable it.

steps.title: Set up the consent screen
steps.plain: Your users see this 'Allow?' page. Enter the name of your app and a support email. Select 'External', so that people outside your company can connect.
steps.technical: Go to Google Auth Platform > Get started. For Audience, select External (any Google user) or Internal (only your Workspace organisation). Add your home page, privacy policy and authorized domains.

sources.title: Google: Configure the OAuth consent screen

steps.title: Create the OAuth client
steps.plain: Create a 'Web application' client. Add the callback address of your app as an authorized redirect URI.
steps.technical: Go to Clients > Create client > Web application. In Authorized redirect URIs, add your callback address. It must be exactly the same as the `redirect_uri` that your code sends.

sources.title: Google: OAuth 2.0 for web server apps

steps.title: Keep the client ID and secret in your app
steps.plain: Create a client secret. Keep the secret and the client ID in the secret store or environment variables of your app.
steps.whyHuman: The secret is the password for your app. Paste it yourself. Then it does not go into the chat history of an agent.

steps.title: Add test users and try it
steps.plain: When the app is in 'Testing', only the people on your list can connect. They see a warning screen. Add the email addresses of your team. Then try a connection.

steps.title: Prove you own your domain
steps.plain: Verify your company domain in Google Search Console. Usually, you add a DNS record.
steps.whyHuman: This step needs access to the DNS settings of your domain.

steps.title: Publish a privacy policy and record a demo video
steps.plain: Put your privacy policy on the same domain as your home page. The policy must tell how you use Google data. Record a video of the sign-in steps. The video must show how you use each restricted permission. Upload it to YouTube as Unlisted.
steps.whyHuman: The policy is a legal promise. The video must show your real app. An agent can write a draft of both. You then examine them.

link.label: Open YouTube Studio to upload as Unlisted

steps.title: Submit for verification
steps.plain: Fill in the verification form. For each restricted permission, tell why you need it. Tell why a smaller permission does not work. Attach the link to the video.

steps.title: Google reviews your app
steps.plain: First, Google examines your branding. This takes 2 to 3 business days. Then Google examines the restricted permissions. Google says that this 'can potentially take several weeks'.

evidence.note: Google says 'several weeks'. The range of 14 to 42 days is our estimate. It is not a Google number.

steps.title: Get a security assessment (each year)
steps.plain: Some apps get restricted Gmail data through a server, not only in the browser of the user. These apps need an assessment by an assessor that Google approves. If your server gets email for your agent, this applies to you. The Google Trust and Safety team tells you when to start. You do the assessment again each 12 months.
steps.whyHuman: You select and pay an assessor. You answer the questions of the assessor.

evidence.note: Google gives no cost or duration. The range of 7 to 30 days is our estimate.

forks.effect: Google calls permission to send 'sensitive', not 'restricted'. Google must still verify your app. But you do not need a security assessment. This is much faster.

forks.condition: Only people inside your own Google Workspace will connect
forks.effect: Select 'Internal' on the consent screen. Google does not verify the app.

forks.condition: You do not verify the app (a test with a small number of users)
forks.effect: Users see an 'unverified app' warning. A maximum of 100 new users can connect in total. In Testing mode, sign-ins also expire sooner.

evidence.note: Google says that refresh tokens in Testing mode have a limited life. We did not check the usual value of 7 days again.

nuances.title: Ask for the smallest Gmail permission
nuances.detail: Google calls these permissions restricted: gmail.readonly, gmail.modify, gmail.compose, gmail.metadata and full mail access. gmail.send is only sensitive. Google asks you to tell why a smaller permission does not work.
nuances.ifStuck: If your agent only writes drafts or sends email, remove the permissions to read. Then you do not need the security assessment.

nuances.title: Verification again each year
nuances.detail: Apps with restricted permissions must get a new assessment each 12 months. If you add a new restricted permission, you can need a new assessment.
nuances.ifStuck: When your approval letter comes, put the renewal date in your calendar.

nuances.title: Your app is unverified during the review
nuances.detail: Until Google approves the app, only test users on your list can connect. Or, a maximum of 100 new users can connect after a warning screen.
nuances.ifStuck: Start the verification early. During the wait, do pilots with the test users on your list.

config.redirectUriNote: Add the callback address of your app as an authorized redirect URI on the OAuth client.

scopes.name: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.modify
scopes.plain: Read, change and delete email. It cannot delete email permanently.

useCases.label: Read, sort or draft replies to email
useCases.summary: Restricted access. Google verifies the app. A third party also does a security assessment each year.

useCases.label: Send email only
useCases.summary: gmail.send is sensitive, not restricted. Google verifies the app. You do not need a security assessment.

evidence.note: Google gives the permission class. Google gives no duration for this verification. The wait is our estimate.

useCases.label: Only people in your own Google Workspace
useCases.summary: Set the app to Internal. Google does not verify the app.

composio.note: Users can connect today through the Composio Gmail app. Use it while you set up your own app or wait for the review. Users see 'Composio' on the approval screen. Other Composio customers share the same rate limits. Polling triggers run a maximum of one time in 15 minutes. Change to your own app when it is ready.

limits.note: The Composio Gmail docs do not list the permissions of the Composio app. The docs say that Google blocks permissions that it did not verify for that app. Connect a test account through Composio. Make sure that the actions of your agent work before you use it.

evidence.note: The toolkit page shows that Composio has its own app. It does not show the permissions of that app.

existingApp.summary: Add the callback address of your agent to your existing OAuth client. Or, create a second client in the same project. With the two methods, you keep the verification of your project. This is true only if you do not change the permissions.

reReviewTriggers.trigger: You add a restricted permission that Google did not verify
reReviewTriggers.effect: Google verifies the app again. A new restricted permission can also need a new security assessment.

reReviewTriggers.trigger: You change the app name, logo or domains that users see
reReviewTriggers.effect: Google does the brand verification again. This usually takes 2 to 3 business days.

reReviewTriggers.trigger: You add a second client in the same project
reReviewTriggers.effect: The second client uses the same consent screen. Thus, it probably does not need its own verification.

evidence.note: This is our conclusion about how verification applies to the consent screen of the project. The page does not say it directly.

blockers.symptom: The automatic brand check of Google shows problems
blockers.cause: Your home page must be public, with no login. It must tell what the app does and link to the privacy policy. The privacy policy must be on the same domain. It must tell how you use Google data. You must verify your domain in Google Search Console.
blockers.fix: Correct each problem on the list. Then start the verification again. Or, request a manual review. This usually takes 2 to 3 business days. Before you change your branding, cancel the verification. After a pass, publish the app in 7 days or less.

blockers.cause: The Google Trust & Safety team can send you an email to get more data. The review stops until you reply.
blockers.fix: Examine the inbox of the developer contact and support addresses on your consent screen. Examine the spam folder too. In the Verification Center, look for a paused status. Reply in the same email thread.

escalate.label: Google: verification and Trust & Safety follow-up

blockers.symptom: Google refuses verification because of a policy flag
blockers.cause: Google flagged a project on your account for a Terms of Service violation. Or, Google Search marks your domain as dangerous.
blockers.fix: Correct the flagged project and send an appeal in the Google Cloud console. Or, correct the problems in Search Console and request a security review. Send the app again only after that review is complete.

sources.title: Google Cloud: Examples of common issues

authorize.detail: Sign-in endpoint answers and rejects a made-up app ID: "Authorization Error The OAuth client was not found."

discovery.detail: The provider's published OAuth configuration lists the same sign-in address.
